objections.claim: The check only scans for explicit `AsExpression` and `TypeAssertionExpression` nodes. But the spec's own boundary functions (`readJson`, `readLedgerEntries`, `parseJsonlEntries`) return `any` today. Assigning that `any` to a typed `GovernedRecord`/`AdmissionRecord` (whose `producer_id`/`contract_revision` are pinned to `string`) is an implicit cast that the AST walker will never flag. The spec's DONE item "no `as`/`<T>` crossing a boundary" is therefore satisfied vacuously on the ledger path, while the actual boundary crossing (the `any` assignment) is unguarded.
objections.evidence: Spec §3 "Validated input boundaries" explicitly lists "on-disk JSON/JSONL (`readJson` line 93, `readLedgerEntries`/`parseJsonlEntries`…)" as a boundary. Spec §3 "Brands flow at every boundary" states "`readJson`/`readLedgerEntries`/`parseJsonlEntries` return `any` today". Spec §3 "Cast-prohibition check" defines the check as collecting "every `AsExpression` and `TypeAssertionExpression` node" — it does not collect implicit `any`-to-typed assignments.
objections.predicted_consequence: A developer can write `const rec: GovernedRecord = readJson(...)` and the check passes, silently erasing the brand at the ledger read. The `tsc` error the spec promises for an un-minted `string` reaching `deriveKey` never fires, because the `any` assignment launders the type before the validator is ever called. The core load-bearing model ("brands flow on the ledger path") is not actually enforced by the shipped mechanism.

objections.claim: The project `tsconfig.json` has `include` listing only the two `.ts` files (`producer-auth.ts`, `commissaire.ts`). The S2 fixture is a third, standalone `.ts` file. If the test invokes `tsc --noEmit` with the project tsconfig, the fixture is excluded from compilation and the test silently passes (or fails to compile the fixture at all). If the test passes the fixture path explicitly to `tsc`, it is no longer "under the project `tsconfig.json`" — it uses a different compilation context, which can change resolution and option semantics.
objections.evidence: Spec §3 "Toolchain" states "`include` lists only the two `.ts` files". Spec §5 S2 states the fixture is "Compiled with `tsc --noEmit` under the **project `tsconfig.json`**".
objections.predicted_consequence: The S2 test either becomes a no-op (the fixture is never type-checked, so the `TS2345` assertion never runs) or requires a separate tsconfig/CLI invocation that contradicts the spec's explicit instruction. The brand-flow proof is not actually exercised by the described test harness.

objections.claim: `allowJs` is set in `tsconfig.json`, but `include` lists only the two `.ts` files, so `allowJs` has no effect on the build. `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` is explicitly admitted to be "inert here" because all relative specifiers are extensionless. Keeping both options in the committed config invites future maintainers to assume they are load-bearing and to reason about the toolchain from a false model.
objections.evidence: Spec §3 "Toolchain" lists `allowJs` and `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` among the `compilerOptions`, and states the latter "is **inert** here". The same section defines `include` as "lists only the two `.ts` files".
objections.predicted_consequence: A future contributor sees `allowJs` and assumes `.js` files are part of the compilation input, or sees `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` and adds a `.ts`-suffixed import expecting it to be rewritten — both actions would fail or behave unexpectedly, requiring a debugging session against the actual (different) semantics.

objections.claim: The spec's central behaviour-preservation claim — a malformed ledger/admission record (non-string or empty `producer_id`/`contract_revision`) must yield the same deny/skip/failure outcome as today, never a new throw — is a DONE item with no scenario and no named test. S4b's "every existing commissaire + producer-auth test passes" cannot cover it: no existing test feeds a malformed `producer_id`/`contract_revision` into `verifyAuthLeg`/`evaluateDecisionRequest` (the selftest's tampered-record case uses a valid `producer_id` with a bad HMAC; the parity tests use valid flags). The same gap applies to the CLI fail-loud path: `asProducerId` is introduced for `--producer`, but no test covers a malformed (empty) flag value — the parity tests cover *missing* flags, not *malformed* values, so a conversion that turns the current exit-2 usage error into an uncaught throw passes every named AC.
objections.evidence: DONE item 5/6 ("mapping `null` to the existing deny/skip… no new throw"); §3 "Brands flow at every boundary"; S4b; the parity tests in `test/commissaire-standalone.test.mjs` (missing-flag cases only).
objections.predicted_consequence: A build that maps `tryAsProducerId(null)` to a throw, or to the wrong reason string, passes every named AC. Concretely: today a non-string `producer_id` in the ledger yields `verifyAuthLeg` failure reason `producer-auth-mismatch`; the spec's wording "the existing deny/skip/`producer-auth-failed` outcome" names a *different* string, and if the conversion maps `null` to it, `audit verify`'s output changes observably. With no test asserting the reason string or the no-throw property, done cannot be decided for this AC.

objections.claim: "faff commissaire --selftest startup recorded on this ticket for source and emit" is decidable only as "the numbers appear on the ticket"; there is no threshold, comparison, or regression bound that makes it pass/fail.
objections.predicted_consequence: A build that records any two numbers satisfies the AC regardless of whether the source lane regressed startup by 10×; done is decidable (ticket contains numbers) but vacuous — the AC cannot distinguish a good from a bad outcome.
